doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Too much information, fewer distinctive voices
summary: Rowe and Maricle lament that younger players are hard to tell apart, unlike Armstrong, Lester Young or Hodges.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Isn’t that interesting how the amount of information available — is there some kind of ratio to innovation I guess. It almost doesn’t make it easier because there’s so much there. I can’t even finish my thought but I guess I almost long for some of the old days when things just seemed to be more spontaneous or from the heart.

And you could hear a player and in a second you’d know who it was. You’d know instantly if it was Louis Armstrong or Clark Terry or the difference between Dexter Gordon or Lester Young or whatever, and Johnny Hodges and Phil Woods, something totally extreme. But you could always tell right away without even — you know now, we were saying before, especially with the younger players, you listen and I would, if I took a blindfold test on new players I’d completely fail. I’d have no idea of how to identify except by tune, if you know someone’s tune, but not by their soloing style necessarily. So much of it sounds the same.
